items.title: The Relationship That Can Survive Not Talking for Years
items.description: If you don’t speak with a relative for years, you’re probably estranged. If you’re dating someone who’s dropped contact for the past month, you’ve been ghosted. You haven’t heard from your boss in six months? Uh-oh. But one kind of relationship seems to consistently defy the laws of interpersonal physics: friendship. When friends reunite, the fabric of time can pleat seamlessly, allowing them to simply, as the saying goes, pick up where they left off. “Time doesn’t take away from true friendship, nor does separation,” Tennessee Williams wrote in Memoirs . “When we’re together, the years fall away,” Judy Blume once wrote of her best friend, Mary. In the 100 interviews with groups of friends that I conducted for my series The Friendship Files , I often heard similar sentiments. “It was like we’d never been apart,” one person told me of reconnecting with his Army buddies after more than a decade. “It’s as if nothing has changed,” another said of their relationship with friends from kindergarten . If friendship has a superpower, it is the time travel of reconnection. Before these moments, sometimes weeks, months, or years pass with only sporadic communication, if not complete silence. Yet through these fallow periods, friendship can persist without diminishing in strength. I’ve come to think of these empty spaces as friendship’s dark matter. It is the part of friendship we can’t see, directly measure, or definitively prove exists—but we know it’s there, and we feel its effects. In a 1991 paper , Stuart Sigman, a communication researcher, emphasized the importance of the part of relationships that happens in the silence between interactions. “Relationships do not cease after the face-to-face events (conversations) engaged in by co-members are terminated,” he wrote. “In a sense, relationships are ‘larger’ than the physical presence or interactional accessibility of the participants.” Although all relationships have some of this dark matter, friendship is unusual because of how much silence it can survive. Someone doesn’t necessarily lose the title of “friend” just because you haven’t talked to them in a while. With family or romantic partners, a reunion after a long separation could be expected to bring some drama. Yet seeing an old friend is often described as frictionless. [ Read: How friendships change in adulthood ] The nature of friendship allows for this goodwill. “Freedom lives at the heart of friendship,” William Rawlins, an emeritus professor of communication at Ohio University, told me. You can’t choose your parents, but every friendship is created from scratch by the participants themselves. It can take any form they imagine. Cultures have shared expectations for how romantic relationships progress and when families ought to gather. Although couples and families don’t necessarily conform to those scripts, they’re still aware of them. Those cultural guideposts barely exist for friendship. There is no universal prescription for how often friends ought to talk to or see one another. “Our friendship is going to exist as long as we are living up to each other’s expectations of the friendship,” Rawlins said. Friendships can go dormant for a while without dying, he wrote in his 1992 book, Friendship Matters , so long as all parties still think of one another as friends: “The unspoken in friendship, its shared image, may excuse former neglect.” So what is happening when nothing is happening between friends? This is the question Kinneret Lahad, a professor of women’s studies at Tel Aviv University, explored in a paper she published last year. The short answer, as she wrote, is that when nothing happens, “everything happens at the same time.” The full answer is more complicated. “Friendship is imbued with so many sensations, so many intensities that cannot be quantified or qualified or represented in narratives,” Lahad told me. (I’ll try my best to represent some of them in this narrative nevertheless.) Nothing visible or measurable may be happening between two friends; they may be, by all appearances, out of touch. But perhaps they think of each other often. Maybe one helped the other find a job that took them to a new place many years ago; their whole life trajectory remains shaped by that friendship, even though they’re now apart. One friend might see something that makes them think of the other, wonder whether they should reach out, and almost do it, only to hesitate at the last moment. Any or all of that could be happening when a friendship appears dormant. “When nothing is happening in friendship, all of friendship’s ambiguities, possibilities, and constraints are laid bare,” Rawlins said. Lahad’s point is that all of these almosts, maybes, and intangible thoughts still matter. They still affect the friendship and the people within it. This dark matter can, like the universe’s, be the glue that keeps friends together, or it can be the shadows in which misunderstandings and resentments fester. One indirect piece of evidence for the existence of friendship dark matter is that the feeling of closeness between friends is not necessarily linked to how often they are in touch. In a study of long-distance and geographically close friends, Amy Janan Johnson, a professor of communication at the University of Oklahoma, found that although far-flung friends did fewer “maintenance behaviors”—such as calling each other, joking around together, and offering emotional support—that did not mean they felt less connected or invested in the relationship. In fact, she told me, some long-distance friends’ commitment to the relationship was “still increasing.” Johnson suggested that in addition to the active maintenance of talking to and seeing one another, people might also engage in passive maintenance of their friendships by, for instance, looking at old photos and feeling fond feelings, or thinking of someone and wishing them well. These things seem small and ephemeral, but they are ways that friendship can be present even in absence. And they may contribute to the feeling, upon reunion, that the friendship was never interrupted at all. [ Read: Want closer friendships? Move away from your friends. ] Lahad recently published another paper , with her friend and co-author Klara Goedecke, about the feeling of reconnecting after a period of nothingness. And in the most scholarly way possible, they basically said that it’s magic: “Sensed suspension of the sociotemporal order that would otherwise cast time apart as rupture has a ‘mythical’ or ‘extra-temporal’ quality,” they wrote, “which we conceptualize as a sense of wonder.” This wonder is not guaranteed . Let us not over-romanticize the flexibility of friendship; it is completely possible that the dark matter contains not the comforting certainty of continued connection, but confusion and hurt. Friends can drift apart over long separations, and reuniting may be awkward rather than smooth. “Meeting up with an old friend constituted a friendship trial,” Lahad and Goedecke wrote, “a moment where the friendship was put to the test, as it were.” Reconnection comes with risk. Although you may have thought that everything was fine, that it was mutually understood that you still loved each other through the silence, your friend might be upset with you for not reaching out. “Treasured old friendships persist partly as vital (and hopefully mutual) fantasies,” Rawlins wrote. The risk is that the fantasy is not mutual. As technology has made keeping in touch easier and easier, the dark matter of friendship may feel heavier than it did in previous generations. Rawlins and Johnson both pointed out that for those who didn’t grow up with the internet and social media, and had only calls and letters to bridge the distance, long silences between friends may have felt more benign. Friends have so many ways to reach out to one another now that it may feel more fraught when they don’t. This sense that reconnection is risky could be why, as a couple of studies have found , people tend to be reluctant to contact their old friends. Even when they say they’d like to, many hesitate to actually do it. But the risk may not be as high as they think. Another study found that people tend to consistently underestimate how happy those in their social circle are to hear from them. What makes a friendship more or less likely to pick up where it left off? Kristina Castaneto, a psychology Ph.D. student at Simon Fraser University, in Canada, is trying to investigate what makes a person more likely to reconnect with an old friend; her adviser, Lara Aknin, worked on the study about reluctance to reach out. In a recent study , they could not find any personality traits that were linked to someone’s likelihood of getting back in touch. The only thing that seemed to move the needle was a new concept they’ve come up with: friendship resiliency, which they define as “the belief that the friendship will remain despite how much time has passed,” Castaneto told me. That sounds, essentially, like a belief in friendship dark matter. She is still working on developing a way to reliably measure this concept. But it seems possible that the very thing that brings friends back together might be the belief that they’re never truly separated, even when they’re apart. Yet I can’t help but wonder how much this phenomenon is a special property of friendship, and how much it is a survival mechanism in a culture that puts friendship last. Lahad said that she and Goedecke got a similar critique from a colleague regarding their paper on reconnection and wonder. People should be working on their friendships, this person said, not coasting on the assumption that the time apart will collapse when they get back together. The dominant values of American culture—and many other cultures—still say that you should prioritize your work and your family before your friends. When friendship is expected to make way for these other things, people may get used to tolerating lapses in contact, or think that they have no choice but to accept them as part of friendship. The “assumption of benevolence” through a dormant period, as Rawlins put it, can be a beautiful part of friendship. But “at the same time, Julie, at some point, you kind of have to live that with each other,” he told me. You have to prove the benevolent assumption correct. You have to actually pick up where you left off. That’s the thing about friendship dark matter—it can hold the visible matter together … so long as there is some visible matter. Friendship does require taking action, at some point, if you want it to be more than a fond memory. But it is more than the sum of the actions taken. Even if you do make your friends a priority, even if you are regularly in touch, the magic, unmeasurable dark matter remains. Lahad told me about a woman she’d interviewed whose friend had offered her a room to stay in when she was thinking of divorcing her husband. She never took her friend up on it, but just knowing that she had that safety net if she needed it helped give her the confidence to take action and get divorced. Something that wasn’t actually happening was shaping everything. “Friendship also exists in these ways that cannot be boiled down only to how often we meet and how often we talk,” Lahad said. In the dark matter, there is uncertainty, yes. But, as Rawlins said, “the other side of uncertainty is faith.”

items.title: Faso Talent d’or 2026 : Chérifa Sanon décroche le grand prix d’une valeur de 2 millions de FCFA
items.description: La 4e édition de la compétition Faso Talent d'or 2026 a refermé ses portes avec la cérémonie de remise de prix aux lauréats, le samedi 21 novembre 2026, à Ouagadougou. Au terme de cette cérémonie, la créatrice de contenu Chérifa Sanon a été sacrée Faso Talent d'or 2026. Elle repart avec une récompense de 2 millions de FCFA. Après une première phase de sélection marquée par les votes du public, le suspense a pris fin avec la proclamation des résultats. Parmi les candidats en lice, Chérifa Sanon s'est particulièrement illustrée en remportant le grand prix de cette quatrième édition. Ahmed Yessoufou, le promoteur du Faso Talent d’or s’est exprimé satisfait Pour le promoteur du Faso Talent d'or, Ahmed Yessoufou, cette édition est une source de satisfaction au regard du déroulement de la cérémonie. « C'est un sentiment de satisfaction pour tout ce qui s'est passé. Ce fut une belle soirée. Tout le monde est reparti avec son trophée et son enveloppe », a-t-il confié. Selon le promoteur, le Faso Talent d'or entend mettre en lumière des talents qui peinent parfois à bénéficier de la visibilité qu'ils méritent. S'adressant aux candidats, Ahmed Yessoufou a salué leur engagement et les a encouragés à poursuivre leurs efforts. « Être nominé, c'est déjà une victoire. Repartir finaliste, c'est une deuxième victoire, et repartir lauréat, c'est une consécration », a-t-il déclaré. Sacrée Faso Talent d'or 2026, Chérifa Sanon n'a pas caché sa joie. Créatrice de contenu et promotrice d'une marque de vêtements, elle considère cette distinction comme une reconnaissance de son travail et de sa passion. « Je remercie le comité d'organisation parce que j'ai été nominée dans la catégorie créatrice de contenu. C'est quelque chose que je faisais par passion. Voir qu'aujourd'hui je suis finaliste et que je remporte le prix de Talent d'or de l'année, je suis vraiment honorée », a-t-elle exprimé. Chérifa Sanon, sacré Faso talent d’or décide de consacrer la moitié du montant reçu pour des œuvres caritatives La lauréate consacre ses contenus à la valorisation de la culture et du patrimoine. Ses publications mettent notamment en avant les activités culturelles, les sites touristiques et les richesses du Burkina Faso. Chérifa Sanon a confié qu'une partie du montant remporté sera consacrée à une activité communautaire en faveur des personnes dans le besoin, tandis que l'autre partie servira à acquérir du matériel de meilleure qualité afin d'améliorer ses productions audiovisuelles. Outre le grand prix, plusieurs autres distinctions ont été décernées au cours de la soirée. Il s'agit notamment des prix du meilleur jeune artisan, du meilleur jeune entrepreneur innovant, du meilleur artiste de l'année, du meilleur acteur de l'industrie culturelle et créative, de la femme d'impact, du meilleur créateur de contenu, du meilleur créateur de mode (catégories designer et crochet), du meilleur jeune photographe, du meilleur jeune talent du micro et du meilleur acteur du 7e art. Dans chacune de ces catégories, les lauréats ont reçu un trophée, une attestation et une enveloppe de 200 000 FCFA. Remise d’attestation au meilleur photographe de l’année Notons que le Faso Talent d'or est une initiative déployée dans quatre pays, à savoir le Gabon, le Togo, la Côte d'Ivoire et le Burkina Faso. À travers cette compétition, les organisateurs ambitionnent de célébrer les talents, de promouvoir leur savoir-faire et de leur offrir une meilleure visibilité. Sakinatou ZOUNDI Minute.bf

items.title: PTI MNAs demand to know whereabouts of party leaders detained in KP, seek their court production
items.description: ISLAMABAD: PTI lawmakers from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Sunday reiterated their demand for the immediate disclosure of the whereabouts of all detained PTI leaders and workers, their production before the courts and the provision of their legal right to defence. The demand was made during a meeting of PTI’s elected members of the National Assembly (NA) from KP, held in Islamabad under the prevailing political and constitutional situation, according to a statement by the party. At the meeting, the lawmakers called for the immediate disclosure of the whereabouts of now non-functional chief minister Sohail Afridi, KP Assembly Speaker Babar Saleem Swati, provincial president Junaid Akbar Khan and other detained party leaders and workers. Afridi — whose role as the chief minister was rendered non-functional due to governor’s rule — Swati and some other lawmakers have been in “ preventive detention ” since emergency was imposed, according to police. KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi also said last month that Afridi and Swati had been placed under house arrest . The lawmakers expressed serious concern over the alleged arrests and undisclosed whereabouts of Afridi, Swati, Junaid Akbar Khan, MNAs Dr Amjad, Fazal Muhammad Khan, Naseem Shah, Iqbal Afridi and Zubair Wazir, along with provincial ministers and MPAs. They demanded that all detained elected representatives be immediately brought before the public and produced before the relevant courts. “Their families should be informed about the reasons for their arrests and places of detention, while they must be granted the full legal right to defend themselves,” the statement said. The PTI members stressed that depriving elected representatives of their political activities and keeping them in undisclosed detention amounted to an assault on democratic values and the public mandate. In last month’s comments on detentions after governor’s rule, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry had said those with cases against them will be tried, while others would be released. The participants also condemned the recent detentions of former provincial minister Taimur Saleem Jhagra, Kamran Bangash and Irfan Saleem under the MPO, asserting that their arrests despite protective bail granted by the Peshawar High Court raised serious questions about respect for judicial orders and the rule of law. The PTI lawmakers demanded that the three leaders be immediately produced before the court, released and provided with all legal facilities, the statement said. Former National Assembly speaker Asad Qaiser, along with MNAs Atif Khan, Saleem Rehman, Sahibzada Sibghatullah, Mehboob Shah, Shahram Khan Tarakai, Shahzada Gastasap, Muhammad Nawaz Khan, Asif Khan, Ali Asghar Khan, Arbab Sher Ali, Sohail Sultan, Ali Khan Jadoon, Sajid Momand, Shah Ahad and Bashir Khan, attended the meeting. The PTI statement comes a day after it emerged that President Asif Ali Zardari promulgated an ordinance, doing away with most of the “privileges” of KP lawmakers, including protection against “preventive detention”. Through an amendment ordinance related to the privileges of MPAs, drastic changes have been made in the KP Provincial Assembly (Powers, Immunities and Privileges) Act 2026, as 21 of its 40 sections have been omitted, including those providing protection to the MPAs against “preventive detentions” and offences related to “breach” of privileges. Four other ordinances promulgated provided a legal framework for special initiatives in the designated 12 districts and other districts in the province. With the imposition of emergency in KP on Oct 11, an Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) was formed to oversee 12 districts that were deemed to face intense security challenges, including the merged districts. On governor’s rule and ongoing political situation The meeting also condemned reported raids on the homes of PTI workers and detentions under MPO following the imposition of governor’s rule in KP on Oct 11. The participants alleged harassment of political workers, violation of the sanctity of homes and restrictions on political activities, condemning them as “blatant violations of the Constitution and fundamental human rights”. They demanded the immediate release of all detained party workers. Rejecting the imposition of governor’s rule in KP on the pretext of terrorism, the meeting asserted that the PTI provincial government had consistently adopted a zero-tolerance policy against terrorism. The participants said terrorism could not be “used as a political tool to undermine the democratic mandate” of the province. They called for the immediate and effective implementation of the National Action Plan and strict adherence to a resolution adopted by all political parties in KP. During the meeting, PTI leaders claimed that governor’s rule had further aggravated the province’s political, economic and administrative challenges. It also criticised KP Governor Kundi, saying that instead of representing the federation and playing a constructive role in resolving provincial issues, his actions were further complicating the situation. The participants expressed “serious concern” over delays by the federal government in releasing KP’s financial entitlements and deductions from its resources. They said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had promised Rs160 billion to the province, but under a new agreement, the federal government had made deductions of approximately Rs157bn, which they termed an injustice to the people of the province. According to the statement, they contended that the federal government was “treating the province like a stepchild” under the pretext of governor’s rule and stressed that the people of the province could not be deprived of their constitutional and financial rights. The meeting also expressed concern over the withdrawal of security provided to JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman. The participants maintained that ensuring the security of all political leaders, irrespective of political differences, was the responsibility of the state. They demanded that Fazl and other leaders of his party be immediately provided with the required security. The participants welcomed PPP scion Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s statement describing Imran as a political prisoner and his support for PTI’s position on the reserved seats issue. They termed Imran a major political stakeholder and said that attempts to exclude him from the political process were detrimental to democracy. They stressed that the PPP should go beyond statements and take practical steps, calling for Bilawal to dissociate himself from the imposition of governor’s rule and not vote for its extension in the NA. The meeting concluded with a “reaffirmation of the participants’ commitment to the supremacy of the Constitution and the rule of law, the protection of political freedoms, safeguarding the province’s constitutional and financial rights, respect for the public mandate and ensuring the security of all political leaders”, the statement added. PTI seeks Imran’s access to personal physician According to the statement, the meeting also discussed in detail the health and treatment of incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan, the law and order situation in KP, concerns over the imposition of governor’s rule, the province’s constitutional and financial rights, and the overall political situation in the country. Imran has been in prison since Aug 5, 2023 , while his wife was arrested on Jan 17, 2025 in a separate case in which the couple were sentenced. The IHC has allowed him twice-a-week meetings with his family, lawyers and other associates, but despite multiple court directives , the meetings have been largely restricted . Imran and Bushra’s lawyers were able to meet the couple earlier this month after a gap of several months , after the Islamabad High Court issued directives for the meeting to aid legal consultation. In the meeting, PTI lawmakers demanded that all facilities be provided to Imran in accordance with the jail manual and Supreme Court (SC) judgments. They called for him to have immediate access to his personal physician and for the restrictions on meetings with his family, lawyers and political leaders to be removed, maintaining that any negligence or unnecessary restrictions concerning his health and safety would be unacceptable. The meeting also strongly condemned the detention of Imran’s sister Aleema Khan , held since late September under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance (MPO), and demanded her immediate release. It called for Bushra Bibi’s release as well and demanded that she be provided justice in accordance with the law. According to the statement, the participants further demanded that cases against Dr Yasmin Rashid, Shah Mahmood Qureshi, Mahmoodur Rashid, Ejaz Chaudhry and other detained PTI leaders and workers be decided on merit, without political victimisation.

items.title: How ‘Real Food’ Nearly Broke the White House
items.description: In early August, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. staged a “policy celebration” at the Department of Health and Human Services headquarters to give an update on one of his signature initiatives: a new definition of ultra-processed food . Publishing the definition would be the first step toward achieving several “Make America Healthy Again” goals, such as new front-of-package labels to steer consumers away from unhealthy foods and, eventually, a reduction in preventable disease. But even as Kennedy was planning the festivities, a months-long bureaucratic battle was threatening to derail it. Days before the planned event, senior staff at the White House told Kennedy’s team that the definition would need to stay secret because it had not yet cleared a review process at the Office of Management and Budget. That review had become a major point of contention. Some inside the administration wanted more data on the economic effects of policies that could follow from the definition; others insisted that the delay was unnecessary and political. When Kennedy took the stage, flanked by children holding Eat Real Food posters, he could announce only that an announcement was still coming. This dispute over regulatory language has since helped unravel the team that cemented the MAHA-MAGA alliance and has guided Donald Trump for years. Less than two weeks before the midterms, a Kennedy ally named Calley Means quit his job at the White House in protest. White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles then mounted a new effort to release the definition before the election, only to have Kennedy pause it. On the same day that Wiles announced her resignation following a poor Republican showing in the midterm election, Means appeared on Joe Rogan’s podcast to accuse her of caving to the food industry. Inside the White House, some staff were outraged. One White House official that day called Means a liar and a failure who “confuses his own inability to persuade with others’ malfeasance.” Now, under the new regime of Chief of Staff Stephen Miller—who has long claimed his own special affinity for MAHA—the ultra-processed-food language, a draft of which we obtained, is once again moving forward. According to several people with knowledge of the plan, HHS has been preparing again for a long-awaited release of the definition, which is expected as soon as next week. (When asked for comment, HHS directed us to the White House, which sent a statement that listed past MAHA accomplishments and declared, “Stephen Miller and Secretary Kennedy have been working closely together since day one, and they will continue advancing bipartisan MAHA victories.”) The story of the conflagration at the White House, which involves Trump-administration staff trading accusations of corruption and incompetence, is based on interviews with eight current and former officials involved in the process, most of whom requested anonymity to describe conversations that occurred behind closed doors. The dispute exposed major divisions within the White House over how far to take Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again agenda. Now the future of the UPF definition will signal whether the alliance between MAGA and MAHA can survive. The government’s proposed definition of ultra-processed food has remained largely unchanged since a team led by then – Food and Drug Commissioner Marty Makary first drafted it, in the summer of 2025, according to people close to the process. In about 200 words, it classifies as ultra-processed any food or drink containing a chemical preservative, artificial color, added flavor, or low- or no-calorie sweetener such as stevia and aspartame. Additives intended to thicken foods or otherwise alter their texture, such as guar gum and sodium alginate, will also land a food on the UPF list. The definition relies heavily on existing federal regulations that spell out what, exactly, qualifies as a color, sweetener, or other additive. It excludes infant formula, dietary supplements, and foods that qualify as “healthy” under an FDA standard that sets limits on added sugar, sodium, and saturated fat. (Those products also must contain minimum amounts of healthy ingredients such as fruit and whole grains.) Even with those exceptions, experts we spoke with said, the definition of an ultra-processed food would likely cover most packaged products on grocery-store shelves—not just classic junk food, like cheese-filled pretzel bites, but also many flavored yogurts, instant oatmeals, and protein bars. Most packaged breads, which contain additives that prevent mold and maintain softness, would go on the list too. That’s a frightening proposition to the food industry. The Consumer Brands Association, which represents some of the country’s largest food and beverage manufacturers, including PepsiCo and Tyson Foods, argues that the suspected harms of UPFs—obesity, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer—have not been confirmed by strong scientific evidence. It’s true that the science on UPFs, including which ingredients or processes might make them unhealthy, remains unsettled. But nutrition experts told us that enough evidence links them to poor health outcomes that consumers should be warned. That prospect—that the UPF definition will lead to new regulations and legal actions—has been the crux of the fight inside the administration. Kennedy has advocated for new front-of-package UPF labeling that would be similar to cigarette warnings. The Consumer Brands Association has argued that such a requirement would place an undue burden on food manufacturers. The association has touted a recent study by University of Chicago economists predicting that a mandatory label would prompt food companies to spend billions to reformulate their products, raising the average household’s annual grocery bill by $60. But several nutrition experts we spoke with questioned the study’s assumptions. Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutritional epidemiologist, told us that companies are “reformulating and changing their packaging all the time” and still manage to bring in billions in profit. In fact, some companies have done so recently as part of Kennedy’s push to remove artificial dyes from the American food supply. So far General Mills has voluntarily dropped them from cereals sold in the United States, and Kellogg says it plans to ship reformulated Froot Loops and Apple Jacks by year’s end. Food companies are also concerned that a federal definition might be used in litigation. In the past two years, consumers, as well as the city of San Francisco, have sued major food companies over alleged harmful health effects, and advocates hope that a new definition could make their cases more credible. One attorney, John Morgan of Morgan & Morgan, has been especially active in these suits; his firm previously collaborated with Kennedy on an environmental case and maintained a working relationship with him until he became health secretary. That connection “does raise questions in our mind” about Kennedy’s motivations, Rhonda Bentz, a spokesperson for the Consumer Brands Association, told us. Morgan told us that he doesn’t need a new federal definition to help him make a case against food companies but did not rule out incorporating one. “Their defense is always the same one,” he told us. “It’s deny, delay, deny, delay.” Given how vehemently the food industry opposes these measures, some drama over a government UPF definition was inevitable. But at the beginning of the second Trump administration, the two people at the center of the fight nonetheless believed that they could find a solution. Besides Trump and Kennedy, Means and Wiles were the most significant players in the unlikely merger of MAHA and MAGA. Wiles had reached out to Means in 2023 after reading his ideas about public-health reform, and Means first connected Kennedy to Trump. In the weeks that followed, Wiles led the negotiations to merge the Kennedy and Trump campaigns. “Susie Wiles is the best choice of chief of staff for MAHA,” Means posted on X in November 2024, when she was named to the post. In 2025, Wiles green-lighted an aggressive series of reports and announcements in which Kennedy put forward his plans to define ultra-processed food, redesign the food pyramid, and review school and military meals. But Wiles also established a policy process that rankled Means and his allies, allowing different Cabinet departments—as well as lobbyists and industry leaders—to weigh in on changes. “Susie wanted to get to yes, but we had to do it in a way that doesn’t endanger the U.S. food supply,” a government official involved in the policy discussions told us. Means came to believe that the process was just an excuse for further delay, he told us. “The problem with Susie’s leadership was there was no process, and special-interest phone calls were able to delay or kill key priorities that the president ran on,” he said. (Wiles declined to comment for this article.) Kennedy’s staff frequently clashed with farmers, food producers, and Department of Agriculture staff. As we reported in July , MAHA activists inside and outside the administration had become especially frustrated with Heidi Overton, a medical doctor and White House policy adviser, who often slowed down health-policy changes to refine them. Wiles vocally defended Overton and the process at the time, telling us that the White House was focused on making sure “things are correct, legally durable, done with policy consistency.” (Trump nominated Overton to be FDA commissioner in August, but withdrew that nomination earlier this week.) By late last summer, officials at HHS believed that the UPF definition was ready to go. But at an interagency gathering this July, Means was peppered with questions about what the new definition would mean for food prices and the liability of food producers, as well as whether it would be vulnerable to legal challenge, according to people familiar with the meeting. For his part, Means warned other officials that they would be seen as catering to industry interests if they did not embrace the definition, which had then been circulating inside the administration for about nine months. Wiles’s team later insisted that the concerns raised at the meeting had not been addressed. The fact that Republicans were being hammered in campaigns across the country for the rising costs of food also weighed on the White House. Backers of the UPF definition viewed such complaints as stonewalling and were concerned that the delay would endanger their ability to get regulations such as new food labels in place before the end of Trump’s term. “It was two pages,” another person involved in the policy discussions told us. “The idea that you have to do some complex policy process for a two-page proposal is laughable.” Means told us that hundreds of meetings were held to discuss the definition, and he stopped believing that the White House would release one before the election. So he quit. When Means appeared on Rogan’s podcast, he alleged that Wiles had told him that she had concerns about a separate MAHA-coded effort—this one to regulate additives—because Republicans needed money from the sugar industry for the midterms. Allies of Wiles denied that she ever said this, and people who worked with her pointed out that the sugar industry ranked low among top donors to Republican election efforts. The day after his Rogan appearance, Means invited Wiles to sue him. After Means left the White House, Wiles and Kennedy started working again to release the UPF definition so that it could receive public comment before being finalized next year. In the week before the election, the White House and Wiles cleared a version of the definition, including a preamble specifying that it should not yet be used in litigation or for shaping legislation. Then, just days before the election, Kennedy decided that the process was too rushed and opted to wait to announce the language until after the election. The definition that is set to be released now is not expected to be materially different, people involved in the process told us. Kennedy has also carefully kept some distance from the controversy. After Means denounced Wiles as corrupt, Kennedy praised her “inspiring leadership and wisdom” in a post on social media. Trump—who has at times sounded even more aggressive than Kennedy on some MAHA issues, especially those related to childhood vaccines—has remained silent. The White House has not yet announced whether the president will be involved in the release of the new ultra-processed-food standards. Following Means’s departure and the Republicans’ midterms disaster, some pundits were ready to write off MAHA entirely. The unlikely coalition appeared to be fraying, its supporters were demoralized, and most of the candidates backed by its political-action committee lost their race. But MAHA’s obituary may turn out to be premature. A federal UPF definition would be Kennedy’s most tangible win yet, and a sign that MAHA might still have some life left. Assuming, that is, it finally gets published.

items.title: My Apology to American Democracy
items.description: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. A fter any election, it’s natural to hunt for results that prove you were right all along. Landslides in particular provide the winners with ample evidence to sustain just about every prior position. At the moment, Democrats are engaged in a familiar argument over which faction, the progressives or the moderates, can claim responsibility for the party’s remarkable new majority. If you support Medicare for All, you’ll point to Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan. If you’re a skeptic, Roy Cooper of North Carolina won the election’s biggest blowout for a flipped Senate seat. If you want to retire the culture war, look at Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico in Texas. If you thought the race was about Palestine and trans issues, Victoria Broderick just became Tennessee’s first queer member-elect of Congress. Latinos, independents, southern Black women, men under 30, the white working class: bragging rights for all. But it might be more useful to search for what you got wrong. Views that are exploded by subsequent events have a way of disappearing from the mind, making it easy to forget you ever held them in the first place, and creating an illusion that your political wishes always accord with reality. We’re all prone to squeezing facts into the shape of narratives we carry in our heads and ignoring facts that undermine them. These mental habits contribute to a culture of total vindication and no compromise. They also make it difficult to understand present events or predict future ones. Last year, I wrote that America was becoming an authoritarian state. There were grounds for believing it. Think back to the country that America seemed to have become. President Trump ruled with almost no checks on his power. The Supreme Court offered little resistance and Congress none, as if the Constitution had been suspended and the entire federal government had come under the control of one man. The civil service had been gutted, independent agencies neutered, and the Justice Department warped into the president’s personal tool for rewarding friends, punishing enemies, and enriching himself. Long-standing norms of language, behavior, and probity collapsed daily. Elites in business, media, academia, and law lay supine before Trump’s demands for fealty and lucre. After returning to power a man who had tried to nullify democracy, the public seemed entirely passive: content, checked out, or too stunned to react. [ Listen: Autocracy in America ] Remember the fear, the confusion turning to panic. Masked gunmen swept through American neighborhoods, foreigners stayed away from American airports, and international students began to disappear from American universities. After Charlie Kirk’s murder, the White House set out to purge his detractors, and Stephen Miller warned the enemies of goodness—perhaps half the country—that they had awakened a dragon. In red towns, regime critics lowered their voices. In blue cities, families talked seriously about the possibility of moving to another country. Famous figures in the resistance began to leave , while some people I knew tried to parlay a deceased grandparent into a foreign passport and had their children apply to overseas colleges. How could you raise kids here? What if the previous election had returned to power a president who would make sure there would never be another? No one wanted to be the fool who waited too long to get out. But how would you know when it was too late? Having no experience with these dilemmas, we looked to history for guidance. The spirit of the moment was captured in a recent translation of The Oppermanns , written in 1933 by the German Jewish novelist Lion Feuchtwanger, who had the foresight to flee as soon as Hitler came to power. The lesson seemed to be: Get out while you still can. In its annual democracy index for 2025, Freedom House gave the United States its lowest score ever—on par with South Africa and below Panama. Political minds debated what to call this radical deformation of democracy: right-wing populist, illiberal, authoritarian, patrimonialist—even fascist. I wrote an article about this ominous state of affairs with the title “ America’s Zombie Democracy .” Now a free election has delivered an overwhelming rebuke to Trump and his rule. What kind of fascist allows that to happen? I f I were to summarize the flaws in my own thinking, I would say that I overrated Trump’s competence as a dictator, and I underrated the resilience of American democracy. “I don’t think that people were wrong to be worried, and I don’t think the threat is over,” Lawrence Norden, an election-security expert at the Brennan Center for Justice, told me. “I do think maybe some people underestimated the ability to fight back.” Trump wants to rule as a fascist. His governing style emulates the classic features of fascism: cult of the leader, nationalist and xenophobic rhetoric, glorification of the “real” people, demonization of minorities and political opponents, relish for violence, a blizzard of propaganda and lies. Last January, at what was probably the peak of his power following the raid on Venezuela, he declared that only “my own morality, my own mind,” could stop him from doing anything he wanted around the world. But Trump is too shallow, undisciplined, and selfish to lead a great movement with an idealistic vision of the state that can outlive him. He has spent much of his second term distracted by vanity construction projects and self-enrichment schemes. His lifelong attraction to crassly beautiful women has become, in his less priapic ninth decade, an attraction to crassly rich men—Elon Musk, Larry Ellison, Jensen Huang. Trump, his family, and his circle have shown their contempt for the MAGA base by descending into unprecedented depths of corruption at a time of rising prices and interest rates. A competent dictator wouldn’t lose touch with the people whose voice he claims to be. He wouldn’t allow his regime to take the place of the arrogant elites who had served as foils on his way to power. He wouldn’t keep harping on his new ballroom. Trump is a failed fascist. Just as Americans who have known no system other than liberal democracy struggle to imagine its downfall, to understand an authoritarian American president, we tried to compare him to analogues past and present. When Trump was first elected, in 2016, a friend said, “We have to hope he’s Berlusconi, not Mussolini.” Trump is both, and the mix of showman and strongman makes him harder to predict than either one separately. It’s intellectually more straightforward to think of him in the mold of a figure like Vladimir Putin than, say, Alberto Fujimori. It’s also emotionally more satisfying: The lines are clear; the stakes couldn’t be higher; a great battle is on. When, a year ago, I wrote the words “We are living in an authoritarian state,” I felt a shudder of fear and gloom, but also, unmistakably, of excitement. I thought that in his second term Trump would focus single-mindedly on keeping and using power. In the first year he did, and many of us worried that in the second year he might rig or annul the midterms. This wasn’t a far-fetched concern: Trump tried to change voting rules, disqualify registered voters, intimidate election officials with threats of criminal charges, mobilize the Justice Department to challenge results. With election denialists holding key state offices and rogue immigration agents possibly guarding the polls, Trump could keep an irrevocably gerrymandered Congress Republican and harden MAGA’s lock on power. Then he might find a way to continue as president for a third term or install one of his children in the White House. None of this was a fever dream, but it gave Trump too much credit. As it turned out, the midterms held his attention only fitfully. When courts struck down his executive orders, he didn’t defy them. When people in Minneapolis found the courage to protest the thugs with guns who were terrorizing their neighbors and killing American citizens, Trump backed off. Almost on a whim, he started a ruinous war with Iran. While his popularity sank, he went about relining the Reflecting Pool, changing the interior design of the White House ballroom, and enlarging plans for the Triumphal Arch. He spent a lot of time organizing garish celebrations of America’s 250th birthday, claiming it as his own. Actually governing the country hardly seemed to interest him. His appearances in the fall campaign grew more and more bizarre—no one remembers anything from those speeches except a few obscene insults and a peculiar fixation on a Republican senator’s buttocks. Historical analogies pointed to the Roman emperor Caligula. And when, on November 3, the voters gave a shattering blow to Trump and his movement—a loss too big to rig or overturn—his initial response was a shrug. After all, his name wasn’t on the ballot. Within the gilded walls of his own mind, he remained undiminished. Whereas Trump proved unequal to the demands of holding autocratic power, American democracy in 2026 showed a resilience that seemed to have disappeared in 2025. A year ago I thought that little stood between Trump and the consolidation of authoritarian rule. The institutions were hollow and the elites spineless. But this year two of those institutions made sure that the public would have a say: the federal courts and the state and local election system. Almost every attempt by the administration to change voting rules, interfere with election officials, and manipulate the vote count was blocked by the courts, including, in at least one case, the Supreme Court. Election officials around the country resisted the administration’s efforts to intimidate them. Norden, of the Brennan Center, said, “We are lucky that we have a very decentralized election system in the U.S., and the states and civil society were able to take advantage of that to be ready for the assault.” So the people would get a chance to speak. [ Read: How Americans defeated an autocrat-in-waiting ] Despite Trump’s abysmal ratings, I hadn’t forgotten that this electorate returned him to power after he had summoned a mob to try to stop the peaceful transition of power for the first time since the Civil War. Nothing has ever shaken my faith in my compatriots like a presidential election in which the price of eggs mattered more than the fate of democracy. The midterms showed that democracy still matters to most Americans—fitfully, like Trump’s interest in ruling, and not necessarily as a set of abstract concepts called separation of powers , rule of law , and independent judiciary , but in a more visceral way, as a sense of fairness and common decency. Few Americans cared about the destruction of foreign aid by a private citizen who happens to be the richest man in the world. The firing of inspectors general across the federal government aroused little protest. But this didn’t mean that the public had entirely lost its self-respect. Americans who voted for Trump three times were still capable of turning against him. Throughout the year, offense at Trump’s callous excesses slowly rose until it became unstoppable. His greatest mistake was thinking that his spectacular corruption would be of no concern to ordinary people, as if grift on a grand scale came with the divine right to rule. Americans are more likely to ignore abuses of power when times are good. But in a year when health premiums along with the price of gas and diesel spiked, Trump’s gold ballroom and Qatari jet affronted a people who apparently still believe that they are their own masters in a self-governing republic. They just had to be reminded. It was better to exaggerate than underrate Trump’s ability to bring 250 years of democracy to an end. For a distracted and amnesiac people, sleepwalking into authoritarianism remains a risk; the vigilance aroused by Trump’s lawless presidency should be our constant state. But those 250 years have left expectations and habits in American minds that, though they might disappear for a time, are not easily killed.

items.title: Australia: Use Vietnam Dialogue to Press for Rights Reforms
items.description: Click to expand Image Vietnam's President To Lam leads his delegation in a meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at Malacanang Palace in Manila, Philippines, June 1, 2026. © 2026 Rolex Dela Pena/AP Photo (Sydney) – Australian officials should press the Vietnamese government to release political prisoners and reverse its intensifying repression of human rights during the upcoming 21st Australia-Vietnam Human Rights Dialogue, Human Rights Watch said today. The case of an Australian national Tran Hiep, a democracy and human rights activist, is of particular concern. He has been detained in Vietnam since he was reported missing in Cambodia in September 2026. Human Rights Watch urged Australia, in a submission to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, to seek clear, concrete, and measurable progress from Vietnam on issues including political prisoners, labor rights, transnational repression, and freedom of religion and belief. “Since Australia’s last dialogue, Vietnam has sharply intensified human rights abuses both inside and outside the country,” said Daniela Gavshon, Australia director at Human Rights Watch. “Australia needs to make it clear to Vietnam that merely holding another meeting is not itself a measure of progress.” Vietnamese authorities have stepped up transnational repression, reaching beyond the country’s borders to suppress dissent by targeting human rights activists, government critics, and others in violation of their human rights. In late September, the overseas political organization Viet Tan alleged that Vietnamese police had detained three of its members in Cambodia, including Tran Hiep, and transferred them to Vietnam. The Vietnamese government currently holds more than 160 political prisoners for exercising their rights to free expression or for peacefully advocating human rights and democracy. Dozens more are detained and awaiting trial. During the first nine months of 2026, Vietnamese courts convicted and sentenced at least 31 activists to lengthy prison terms, including the prominent bloggers Hoang Thi Hong Thai and Huynh Ngoc Tuan. During this period, the police arrested at least 46 other people for criticizing the government. The upcoming dialogue should also focus on Vietnam’s suppression of independent labor organizing. Both Australia and Vietnam are parties to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, which contains provisions obligating Vietnam to carry out reforms and to allow the creation of independent trade unions. However, as Human Rights Watch recently documented, the Vietnamese government has not actually reformed its policies and practices, and prevents workers from forming and operating genuinely independent unions. The Australian government should communicate concerns about these violations. It should also outline how Vietnam’s failures to reform will affect Australia-Vietnam relations and implementation of trade and tariff provisions in the partnership. “The Australia-Vietnam human rights dialogue will accomplish little so long as concrete outcomes aren’t formalized,” Gavshon said. “A human rights dialogue shouldn’t be a box-ticking exercise but instead a diplomatic exchange with real-world implications.”

items.title: L’Utica plaide pour la promotion de l’huile d’olive conditionnée
items.description: Dans le cadre de l’examen du projet de loi de finances pour 2027, l’Union tunisienne de l’industrie, du commerce et de l’artisanat (Utica) a proposé une série de mesures visant à soutenir l’investissement, la production et l’exportation, notamment dans le secteur oléicole. Les propositions, présentées lors d’une audition conjointe tenue, le vendredi 20 novembre 2026, par la Commission des finances et du budget de l’Assemblée des représentants du peuple et le Conseil national des régions et des districts, dans le cadre de la poursuite de l’examen du projet de loi de finances (PLF 2027),ont porté sur la création d’une structure indépendante dédiée au développement des exportations d’huile d’olive conditionnée, ainsi que sur la mise en place d’un plan national visant à porter la part de ce produit dans le total des exportations d’huile d’olive à 30 %, puis à 50 %. Il convient de savoir que pour la campagne 2025-2026 (novembre 2025 – octobre 2026), l'huile d'olive conditionnée a représenté 15,7 % des volumes et 20,8 % des recettes des exportations tunisiennes d'huile d'olive, selon les données de l'Onagri publiées en novembre 2026. Les représentants de l’Union ont préconisé la mise en place d’une structure indépendante et spécialisée, qui serait chargée de coordonner les politiques et programmes du secteur, de définir les stratégies de promotion et de commercialisation, et d’en assurer le suivi, avec pour objectif de stimuler les exportations et de renforcer le positionnement de la Tunisie sur les marchés mondiaux. À cet égard, ils ont appelé à accélérer la publication du texte réglementaire relatif au rétablissement de la subvention directe à l’exportation, et ce, avant la fin de l’année 2026. I. B. (avec Tap). L’article L’Utica plaide pour la promotion de l’huile d’olive conditionnée est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Veteran journalist Husain Naqi passes away in Lahore
items.description: LAHORE: Veteran journalist and human rights activist Husain Naqi passed away in Lahore on Sunday. He was a former editor of The News and had also been associated with the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP). HRCP official Muhammad Ilyas told Dawn that Naqi died of a cardiac arrest. “He attended a book launch ceremony at the HRCP the previous day. Later, he suffered a heart attack around 6pm on Saturday. He was admitted to a private hospital where he died early in the morning, around 5 am,” Ilyas said, adding that he had left behind three sons. Naqi was buried in Model Town Extension in Lahore. Meanwhile, condolences over his passing continued to pour in. State broadcaster Radio Pakistan reported that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed “deep grief and sorrow over” Naqi’s passing and said it marked the “end of a bright chapter in journalism and democracy”. The premier remembered Naqi as a “principled journalist who fearlessly raised voice for freedom of expression, democratic values and human rights throughout his life”. The prime minister expressed his “heartfelt condolences to the bereaved family, the journalistic community and human rights organisations. He also prayed for the departed soul”, the Radio Pakistan report said. President Asif Ali Zardari also extended his condolences to the bereaved family, expressing “deep sorrow”, a statement issued by the Presidency said. The president paid tribute to Naqi’s “services to journalism, freedom of expression and human rights”, the statement said. It further quoted the president as saying: “Husain Naqi played a prominent role in promoting journalism and democratic values. His contributions will always be remembered.” The HRCP also released a statement, saying it “deeply mourns” Naqi’s passing. “Over a career spanning more than 70 years, from student leader to newspaper editor to treasurer of HRCP, neither multiple incarcerations nor vindictive acts by the authorities ever weakened his resolve to speak truth to power. Naqi sahib served HRCP in different capacities for three decades and was an active council member at the time of his passing. One of the strongest voices for people’s rights and democracy in Pakistan has gone silent,” the statement said. PPP Senator Sherry Rehman posted on X that she was “truly grieved to hear about the sad demise of the veteran journalist and rights campaigner, the iconic Husain Naqi”. “His passing signals the end of an era. Naqi sahib always spoke unflinching truth to power. Many of us cub journalists learnt at his desk, walked in rallies under his leadership. He led so many groups and networks in the hardest days of dictatorship. “We often called him the rebel angel of our times, yet he never stoked anger. He sought the right to dissent with respect. He will be missed. May his soul rest in peace and power,” she said. PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja began his codolence on X by stating: “Alas! Naqi sahib is no longer among us.” He said his acquaintance and admiration for Naqi spanned decades. Naming I.A. Rehman, Asma Jahangir and Amin Mughal along with Naqi, Raja said, “The most precious gems who dreamed of and championed the dignity of human beings and the rising of voices of the poor in Pakistan are leaving us. “Their dreams have yet to be realised. Their dreams are the dreams of 250 million people.” Journalist Absa Komal said Naqi spent his entire life advocating for freedom of speech. “I met him a few months ago at a conference in Karachi, and he still had the same spirit and commitment to the cause. A remarkable life,” she added. Journalist Raza Rumi was more succinct in his message that said: “Rest in peace Naqi sahib.” Former senator Mushahid Hussain Sayed said Naqi was the “last Icon of ‘Old Guard’ progressive journalists” who always spoke truth to power. Who was Husain Naqi? Naqi was born in Lucknow, India before the Independence in 1947. In his autobiography Mujh Se Jo Ho Saka , Naqi said he was perhaps born a year before his officially recorded birthdate in 1936. His great-grandfather had moved to Lucknow from a village in what is now Haryana, in the then-undivided Punjab. It was a well-heeled and well-educated family that flourished in Lucknow over the next few generations. However, Naqi subtly confronted the conservatism of his traditional family from a very young age. Outside, he was not subtle. He began his student activism in secondary school and started taking on the minor establishments of power at a fairly young age. After early schooling and college education in Lucknow, Naqi moved to Karachi in the 1950s, where he developed into a student leader. As a student in Karachi, Naqi played a key role in several demonstrations and protests. During the 1956 Suez Canal crisis when Egypt was attacked by Israel, France and Britain, Naqi was part of the executive committee of the National Students Federation (NSF). At the time, the NSF organised a march to the British High Commission in Karachi to protest against the attack and was faced with police batons and tear gas. As president of Karachi University’s student union, Naqi made a deal with the university’s vice-chancellor for Naqi to be rusticated for three years instead of three Baloch students who had been rusticated in response to an incident at the hostel. Naqi’s activism during his student days was not just centred around protests but also had to do with improving conditions in the institution. He fought for adding a new campus with better facilities, providing safe transport for girls and ensuring that exams were held on time and not postponed. He was a strong advocate for student unions. In an interview published in 2011, he said, “it was the banning of student unions that destroyed campus peace. In our time, student unions were a positive influence. We organised cultural activities. We tolerated diversity. Representatives with various political leanings were able to work together despite their ideological differences”. After a few turbulent years in Karachi, Naqi permanently settled down in Lahore. As a journalist, Naqi found his first mentor in Javed Bokhari, with whom he worked for a couple of years. “In those days I used to literally live at the PPI office,” he had said of the time. He ended up working as the bureau chief of PPI . However, he eventually had to leave the position following a reporting incident in which he refused to accept a false news of desecration of the Holy Quran. Nonetheless, he continued to write for various newspapers, including the Viewpoint , Holiday , Outlook , Frontier Post , Frontier Guardian , Daily Star , Punjab Times and Punjab Punch . Naqi consistently campaigned for the preservation and promotion of the Punjabi language in Pakistan, starting the first-ever daily newspaper in the Punjabi language — Sajjan . Naqi had also been imprisoned a couple of times because of his outspokenness. In the 2011 interview, he recalled those instances with a sense of humour. “I was lucky to invariably have someone favourably disposed towards me at the jail premises, who made sure that I was not mistreated.”

items.title: La République des experts spontanés (Le billet de Samba Oumar FALL)
items.description: Au Sénégal, nous détenons une richesse nationale que les statistiques ne mesurent pas encore : les experts spontanés. Il suffit que le gouvernement vote une loi ou annonce une réforme que le pays se transforme en amphithéâtre. Les constitutionnalistes sortent de Facebook, les économistes émergent de WhatsApp, les juristes s’improvisent sur TikTok et les géopolitologues envahissent les plateaux de télévision. En quelques minutes, chacun maîtrise un texte qu’il n’a parfois même pas lu. Tout le monde explique, interprète, condamne ou applaudit. Le diplôme est accessoire, la compétence facultative, l’assurance obligatoire. Le plus amusant, c’est que l’expertise change de couleur selon le camp. Une décision de son propre camp devient une brillante stratégie. La même, prise par l’adversaire, devient une catastrophe nationale. Chez nous, la science aussi a ses militants. Chacun a certes le droit de donner son avis et de questionner les décisions publiques. Mais avoir une opinion ne revient pas à détenir la vérité. Au fond, nous ne manquons pas d’experts. Nous manquons de rigueur, de documentation et d’humilité. Ici, tout le monde sait tout sur tout. Reste un détail, personne ne sait qui sait vraiment quelque chose. samba.oumar.fall@lesoleil.sn

items.title: France-Algérie : pour Dominique de Villepin, le « temps de la reconnaissance » du passé colonial est venu
items.description: À peine déclarée sa candidature à la présidentielle française de 2027, Dominique de Villepin est allé à contre-courant de la surenchère à laquelle s'adonnent plusieurs candidats de la droite et d’extrême droite concernant la colonisation et la relation avec l'Algérie. L'ancien Premier ministre et chef de la diplomatie sous Jacques Chirac a estimé que le « temps de la reconnaissance » du passé colonial de la France est venu. De même qu'est venu le temps de « tourner la page » et celui « d'inventer un avenir ». Dominique de Villepin : « Notre passé colonial ne passe pas » Pour De Villepin, toutes ces questions qui « enflamment les esprits », comme la colonisation, la relation avec l'Algérie ou la remise en cause des accords de 1968, portent « la marque de quelque chose qui n'a pas été assumé ». « Oui, notre passé colonial, selon la formule consacrée, ne passe pas », a-t-il insisté, soulignant qu'il appartient au chef de l'État « d'assumer le chemin qui permet de regarder en face l'avenir ». « La colonisation, la relation avec l'Algérie qui a enflammé les esprits, la remise en cause des accords de 1968. Tout cela porte la marque de quelque chose qui n'a pas été assumé. Je pense que le temps de la reconnaissance est venu », a-t-il dit. Réitérant que la France est aujourd'hui rattrapée par « cet impensé colonial, par ces débats coloniaux », Dominique de Villepin a estimé qu'il faut « du courage » et « il faut être capable d'être à la hauteur de l'histoire ». « J'ai été à la bonne école auprès de Jacques Chirac », a-t-il rappelé. France-Algérie : Dominique de Villepin refuse la surenchère De Villepin a aussi évoqué le litige lié à l'immigration et aux OQTF. Il trouve « sidérant » que la France bute sur la question de l'immigration et se montre incapable de construire « un traité avec chacun des pays d'origine pour permettre le retour des immigrés qui n'ont pas la place dans notre pays ». Se démarquant nettement du courant anti-algérien qui instrumentalise la relation bilatérale, De Villepin a indiqué qu'il est « inouï de constater que ce n'est que par la surenchère qu'il y aurait des solutions » à l'ensemble des problèmes posés. L’article France-Algérie : pour Dominique de Villepin, le « temps de la reconnaissance » du passé colonial est venu est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Du bagne au Rwanda : l’Occident délocalise ses indésirables (par Moussa DIOP)
items.description: Être aussi efficace que d’essayer de moderniser l’obsolescence, c’est tenter de repousser les frontières migratoires en Afrique. Le 16 novembre, cinq pays européens, l’Allemagne, l’Autriche, le Danemark, la Grèce et les Pays-Bas, ont annoncé un projet de plateforme de retour au Rwanda destinée à accueillir des personnes déboutées du droit d’asile et faisant l’objet de décisions de retour. Une centaine de personnes seraient concernées dans une première phase, à raison d’une vingtaine par pays. Jusqu’où les États occidentaux peuvent-ils externaliser leurs responsabilités en matière de migration et de protection des personnes ? Ce projet marque une nouvelle étape dans la volonté européenne de déplacer hors de son territoire la gestion des personnes dont les demandes d’asile ont été rejetées, y compris lorsqu’elles ne peuvent être renvoyées dans leur pays d’origine. Le contrôle migratoire ne s’arrête désormais plus aux frontières de l’Occident : il tend à s’exercer jusque dans des pays tiers, appelés à prendre en charge une partie de ses conséquences humaines et politiques. Cette stratégie d’externalisation des migrations n’est pas nouvelle. Le projet britannique d’en envoyer au Rwanda, abandonné en 2024, et le dispositif italien en Albanie ont tous deux rencontrés des obstacles juridiques et opérationnels. En avril 2026, les États-Unis ont également transféré quinze migrants latino-américains en Rdc, dans le cadre d’un accord controversé. Pourquoi persister dans cette voie ? Et surtout, quelle efficacité réelle peut-on attendre de dispositifs qui déplacent les personnes sans s’attaquer aux causes profondes des migrations ? Pendant que les gouvernements occidentaux cherchent ainsi à tenir les migrants à distance, les drames se succèdent sur les côtes africaines. Au Sénégal, les derniers épisodes en date portent des noms : Lompoul, où une trentaine de personnes ont péri ; Yène, où quatre corps ont déjà été repêchés et plusieurs dizaines de personnes sont portées disparues ; et Yoff, jeudi soir, où le pire a été évité de justesse grâce à l’intervention de pêcheurs locaux. Autant de tragédies qui rappellent, avec une violence insoutenable, le coût humain de ces traversées vers l’hypothétique Eldorado occidental. Entre ceux qui risquent leur vie pour atteindre l’Europe ou les États-Unis et ceux qui cherchent à organiser leur éloignement depuis l’Occident, une même réalité migratoire révèle ses contradictions et ses impasses. En Europe, l’histoire révèle, à cet égard, un paradoxe saisissant. Pendant des siècles, des puissances aujourd’hui soucieuses d’empêcher l’arrivée de migrants sur leur territoire ont elles-mêmes organisé l’expulsion de populations jugées indésirables vers des terres lointaines. Criminels, pauvres, opposants politiques, dissidents et insurgés étaient expédiés en Australie, en Guyane, en Nouvelle-Calédonie ou en Sibérie pour être éloignés des centres de pouvoir et soustraits au regard des sociétés européennes. Près de 162.000 condamnés britanniques ont ainsi été déportés en Australie entre 1788 et 1868. La France s’est également distinguée d’abord avec le bagne de Guyanne pendant plus d’un siècle (1852-1953) où on peut compter le capitaine Dreyfus parmi ses déportés politiques, mais aussi en faisant de la Nouvelle-Calédonie un lieu de détention des Communards (1872-1897) et des prisonniers de droit commun ; et la Russie tsariste a fait de la Sibérie une immense terre d’exil pour criminels et opposants politiques du 17e au début du 20e siècle. Ces épisodes éclairent d’un jour particulier les débats migratoires contemporains. Hier, des États occidentaux organisaient le déplacement forcé de ceux dont ils ne voulaient plus ; aujourd’hui, ils déploient des politiques de plus en plus restrictives pour empêcher ceux qui aspirent à rejoindre leur territoire d’y entrer. Les contextes, les motivations et les réalités juridiques sont certes différents, car la déportation pénale voire la purge politique ne saurait être confondue avec la migration contemporaine. L’Occident est-il cohérent en s’autoproclamant chantre des droits humains tout en organisant sa mise à distance ailleurs ? La cohérence n’est pas la vertu la mieux partagée au monde. moussa.diop@lesoleil.sn

items.title: Tunisie | Les doléances des opérateurs du BTP
items.description: Dans le cadre de l’examen du projet de loi de finances pour 2027, l’Union tunisienne de l’industrie, du commerce et de l’artisanat (Utica) a proposé une série de mesures visant à soutenir la relance du secteur du bâtiment et des travaux publics (BTP) qui emploie près de 490 000 personnes, soit environ 14 % de la population active occupée dans le pays. Parmi les propositions présentées par la Fédération nationale du bâtiment et des travaux publics, lors d’une audition conjointe tenue, le vendredi 20 novembre 2026, par la Commission des finances et du budget de l’Assemblée des représentants du peuple et le Conseil national des régions et des districts, dans le cadre de la poursuite de l’examen du projet de loi de finances (PLF 2027), la mise en place d’un mécanisme ou dispositif exceptionnel. qui aurait pour tâche de recenser et vérifier, avant le 31 mars 2027, les créances détenues par les entreprises, les bureaux d’études et les fournisseurs sur les organismes publics. Les opérateurs du secteur ont aussi appelé à l’allocation des fonds nécessaires au règlement de ces montants au cours de la même année, prévoyant la possibilité d’opérer une compensation avec les dettes fiscales. Par ailleurs, la Fédération a préconisé la prolongation, jusqu’au 31 décembre 2028, de la mesure d’abandon automatique des pénalités de retard. Elle a également demandé que les entreprises puissent percevoir les montants issus de la révision des prix sans attendre la réception définitive des projets, tout en appelant à l’activation du fonds de garantie des crédits pour aider les petites et moyennes entreprises (PME) à constituer les garanties bancaires requises. I. B. (avec Tap). L’article Tunisie | Les doléances des opérateurs du BTP est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .
